title: Trees
summary: Preorder, inorder, postorder, and level order, and what each order is for.

parts.rule: A tree is a connected acyclic graph with one root. Name the traversal by when you visit the node relative to its children: preorder visits before children, inorder is left-node-right on binary trees, postorder visits after children, and level order walks by breadth with a queue. Each order answers a different question.
parts.why: Problems say "serialize," "evaluate," or "print by level" and candidates walk the wrong order. Preorder rebuilds shape; postorder evaluates children first; inorder on a binary search tree yields sorted keys; level order needs a queue. Mixing them up is an easy silent fail that still "visits every node."
parts.example: Binary tree: root 1, left child 2 with children 4 and 5, right child 3. Preorder visit-then-children: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3. Inorder left-visit-right: 4, 2, 5, 1, 3. Postorder children-then-visit: 4, 5, 2, 3, 1. Level order with a queue: start [1], emit 1 and enqueue 2 then 3; emit 2 and enqueue 4 then 5; emit 3; emit 4; emit 5 — sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If the task is "delete a folder tree," postorder deletes children before the parent so you never remove a directory that still has contents. If the task is "clone the shape," preorder creates the node then recurses into left and right.
parts.use: Use preorder for copy and serialize-with-markers. Use inorder when a binary search tree must emit sorted values. Use postorder for delete, expression evaluation, and leaf-first dependency work. Use level order for distance-by-depth problems and zigzag level prints.
parts.refuse: Refuse inorder on a general non-binary tree without defining a left and right ordering. Refuse ignoring O(n) stack space on a skewed tree of height n. Refuse claiming level order from a recursive preorder walk alone. Refuse treating a DAG as a tree when a child can have two parents.

body:
Rule. A tree is a connected acyclic graph with one root. Name the traversal by when you visit the node relative to its children: preorder visits before children, inorder is left-node-right on binary trees, postorder visits after children, and level order walks by breadth with a queue. Each order answers a different question.

Why it matters. Problems say "serialize," "evaluate," or "print by level" and candidates walk the wrong order. Preorder rebuilds shape; postorder evaluates children first; inorder on a binary search tree yields sorted keys; level order needs a queue. Mixing them up is an easy silent fail that still "visits every node."

Worked example. Binary tree: root 1, left child 2 with children 4 and 5, right child 3. Preorder visit-then-children: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3. Inorder left-visit-right: 4, 2, 5, 1, 3. Postorder children-then-visit: 4, 5, 2, 3, 1. Level order with a queue: start [1], emit 1 and enqueue 2 then 3; emit 2 and enqueue 4 then 5; emit 3; emit 4; emit 5 — sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If the task is "delete a folder tree," postorder deletes children before the parent so you never remove a directory that still has contents. If the task is "clone the shape," preorder creates the node then recurses into left and right.

[[diagram:orders]]

When to use. Use preorder for copy and serialize-with-markers. Use inorder when a binary search tree must emit sorted values. Use postorder for delete, expression evaluation, and leaf-first dependency work. Use level order for distance-by-depth problems and zigzag level prints.

When to refuse. Refuse inorder on a general non-binary tree without defining a left and right ordering. Refuse ignoring O(n) stack space on a skewed tree of height n. Refuse claiming level order from a recursive preorder walk alone. Refuse treating a DAG as a tree when a child can have two parents.
